problem:
Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{10}($
{{field-1}} $)$

examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Definite Integral of a Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts
examples.worked_solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I = \displaystyle \int e^{x}\sin(2x)\, \textrm{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})({e}^{x})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J = \int e^{x}\cos(2x)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula once more, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})({e}^{x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I\mathbin.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}J \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}I) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{4}-\frac{1}{4}I \\ \frac{5}{4}I & =\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-2{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4} \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{{e}^{x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))}{5}){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}))}{5}-\frac{{e}^{0}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot 0)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0))}{5} \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{\pi /2}}{5}+\frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}({e}^{\pi /2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})(-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})(-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}J \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}(-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}I) \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9}-\frac{1}{9}I \\ \frac{10}{9}I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9} \\ \frac{10}{9}I & =\frac{3{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9} \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{10}+C\end{aligned}
$$
